source_text: Λογιζόμενος δέ τις, ὡς καλὸς μὲν ὁ ἥλιος, ἡδὺς δὲ οὗτος ὁ βίος, ἀγαθὸν δὲ καὶ τὸ πολυχρόνιον γενέσθαι διαπαντὸς εὐφραινόμενον, καὶ ὡς φοβερὸν ὁ θάνατος, καὶ ἀΐδιον κακὸν, καὶ εἰς τὸ μηδὲν ἄγων, οἴεται χρῆναι, πάντων μὲν ἀπολαύειν τῶν παρόντων καὶ δοκούντων ἡδέων. Συμβουλεύει δὲ καὶ τοῖς νέοις, τῇ ἑαυτῶν ὥρᾳ καταχρῆσθαι ἀνέντας τὰς ἑαυτῶν ψυχὰς εἰς πᾶσαν ἡδονὴν, καὶ χαρίζεσθαι μὲν ἐπιθυμίαις, πράττειν δὲ τὰ αὐτοῖς δοκοῦντα, καὶ βλέπειν τὰ τέρποντα, καὶ ἀποστρέφεσθαι τὰ μὴ οὕτως ἔχοντα. Πρὸς ὃν τοσοῦτον λέξω· Ὅτι ἀνοηταίνεις, ὦ οὗτος, μὴ προσδοκῶν τὴν ἐφ᾽ ἅπασι τούτοις ἐκ Θεοῦ κρίσιν ἐσομένην. Πονηρὸν δὲ ἀσωτία καὶ ἀσέλγεια, καὶ ῥυπαρὰ σωμάτων ἡμετέρων ὕβρις ὀλέθριος. Νεότητι μὲν γὰρ ἄνοια παρέπεται· ἄνοια δὲ ἄγει εἰς ὄλεθρον.
thought_title: The error of careless living before divine judgment
orientation: The author continues Solomon's voice, confronting a person who calculates that because the sun is beautiful, present life pleasant, and a long joyful life good, while death is dreadful and final, one should enjoy every present pleasure and advise youth to abandon themselves to desire — and warns that this reasoning forgets the coming judgment of God.
pass_a_gloss: Someone reasoning that the sun is beautiful, and this life is sweet, and it is good to be long-lived rejoicing always, and that death is fearful, and an eternal evil, and leading to nothing, thinks it necessary to enjoy all present and seemingly pleasant things. He advises also the young, to use their own time releasing their souls into every pleasure, and to indulge desires, and to do the things that seem good to them, and to look at the delightful things, and to turn away from the things not so. To him I will say this much: That you are senseless, O man, not expecting the judgment from God that will be over all these things. But prodigality and licentiousness are evil, and the destructive insolence of the filth of our bodies. For folly accompanies youth; and folly leads to destruction.

choices.why: Participle with indefinite pronoun introduces a notional person who calculates; 'reasoning' keeps the deliberative force.
ἀνίημι here means to let go, give free rein; 'releasing' shows the active surrender to pleasure.
χαρίζομαι with dative means to gratify, indulge; 'indulge' captures the self-granting sense.
ἀνοηταίνω is a strong rebuke: be devoid of mind, act without understanding; 'senseless' preserves the edge.

choices.english: But prodigality and licentiousness are evil
choices.why: ἀσωτία = wasteful, dissolute living; ἀσέλγεια = shameless excess; both are named as evils.

choices.english: the destructive insolence of the filth of our bodies
choices.why: ῥυπαρὰ = filthy; ὕβρις = insolent outrage; ὀλέθριος = ruinous; the phrase piles shame and ruin on bodily excess.
rejected: the deadly insult of our bodies' filth

bible_refs.note: Rejoice, young man, in your youth... walk in the ways of your heart and the sight of your eyes; but know that for all these God will bring you into judgment.
Remember your Creator in the days of your youth, before the evil days come.
For if a man should live many years, and rejoice in them all; yet let him remember the days of darkness, for they shall be many.

pass_b_english: Someone reasoning might say the sun is beautiful, this life is sweet, and living long while rejoicing continuously is good. They might also say death is terrifying, an everlasting evil that brings one to nothing. Such a person thinks they ought to enjoy all present things that seem pleasant. They even advise the young to use their own time by releasing their souls into every pleasure, to indulge their desires, to do whatever seems right to them, to look at what delights them, and to turn away from what does not. To such a one I will say only this: you are senseless, O man, because you do not expect a judgment from God to follow all these things. But prodigality and licentiousness are evil, and the filthy, ruinous outrage against our bodies is destructive. For folly accompanies youth, and folly leads to destruction.

problems.quote: and the destructive insolence of the filth of our bodies is ruinous
problems.why: 'ῥυπαρά' is an adjective on 'ὕβρις', meaning 'filthy'. The English turns it into a noun, 'the filth of our bodies', and also repeats 'destructive' and 'ruinous'.
problems.fix: and the filthy, ruinous outrage done to our bodies is destructive.

edits.old: and the destructive insolence of the filth of our bodies is ruinous
edits.new: and the filthy, ruinous outrage against our bodies is destructive

fixed: Fixed mistranslation: 'ῥυπαρὰ' modifies 'ὕβρις' (filthy outrage/insolence), not 'σωμάτων'; removed noun-shift 'filth of our bodies' and redundant 'destructive/ruinous' pairing; source reads 'ῥυπαρὰ σωμάτων ἡμετέρων ὕβρις ὀλέθριος' — filthy [insolence] of our bodies, ruinous/destructive.
